article.title: Why ‘Average Customer’ May Describe Almost Nobody
article.why: Understand why averages can hide the real shape of customer behavior.

paragraphs.en:
A report may say that the average customer spends 12,000 yen a month. This sounds useful, but there may be very few customers who actually spend 12,000 yen. An average summarizes a group. It does not always describe a real person.

Imagine five customers who spend 2,000, 3,000, 4,000, 5,000, and 46,000 yen. Their average spending is 12,000 yen, but four of the five customers spend far less than that. The high-spending customer pulls the average upward. If we designed a promotion for an ‘average customer’ who spends 12,000 yen, it might fit nobody very well.

The same problem appears when a population contains different groups. Young customers may visit often but spend less each time, while older customers may visit less often but spend more. The overall average can sit between the two groups even if almost nobody behaves that way.

This does not mean averages are useless. They are helpful for quick summaries and comparisons. The problem starts when we treat the average as a complete picture. A better analysis also checks the median, distribution, percentiles, and important customer segments.

For example, instead of saying only, ‘Average annual spending is 144,000 yen,’ we can add, ‘The median is 82,000 yen, and the top 10 percent account for 45 percent of total spending.’ This gives a more realistic picture of customer behavior.

So when you hear ‘the average customer,’ ask a simple question: does this customer really exist? The average may be mathematically correct while describing almost nobody in the actual population.

For decisions, this matters because different customers may need different actions. One offer can work well for low-frequency customers, while another fits heavy users. Looking at the shape of the data before building a story around the mean helps prevent an imaginary average customer from becoming the center of a real strategy.
paragraphs.zh:
報告可能會說「平均顧客每月消費12,000日圓」，但實際上真正花12,000日圓的人可能很少。平均值是在摘要整體，不一定對應到一個真實存在的人。

假設五位顧客分別消費2,000、3,000、4,000、5,000與46,000日圓，平均剛好是12,000，但五人中有四人遠低於這個數字。高消費者把平均拉高；若依「平均顧客」設計促銷，可能誰都不真正適合。

當母體含有不同群體時也會發生同樣問題。年輕顧客可能來店頻繁但單次消費低，年長顧客可能頻率較低但單次消費高，整體平均會落在兩群中間，卻不代表真的有人以那種方式消費。

這不表示平均值沒用。它適合快速摘要與比較，但不能被當作完整圖像。較好的分析會一起看 median、distribution、percentile 與重要 customer segment。

例如除了「平均年消費14.4萬日圓」，還可以補充「中位數8.2萬，前10%顧客貢獻45%總消費」，這樣更接近實際行為。

因此聽到「average customer」時，應先問：這種顧客真的存在嗎？平均在數學上可以完全正確，卻可能幾乎描述不到任何真實顧客。

這會直接影響施策。低頻顧客與重度顧客可能需要不同 offer；先看資料分布，再用平均建立故事，能避免把一個想像中的平均顧客當成真實策略中心。
paragraphs.ja:
レポートで「平均顧客は月1万2千円使う」と書かれていても、実際に1万2千円使う顧客がほとんどいない場合があります。平均はgroup全体を要約する値で、実在する一人を表すとは限りません。

例えば5人が2千、3千、4千、5千、4万6千円使えば平均は1万2千円ですが、4人は大きく下回ります。高利用者が平均を押し上げており、「平均顧客」向けpromotionは誰にも合わない可能性があります。

複数segmentが混在する場合も同様です。若年層は来店頻度が高く単価が低い、高年層は頻度が低く単価が高いという構造なら、全体平均は両者の中間に位置しても、実際の行動を代表しません。

平均はquick summaryには有効ですが、完全なpictureとして扱うのが問題です。median、distribution、percentile、主要segmentも確認する必要があります。

例えば「平均年間利用額14.4万円」だけでなく、「medianは8.2万円、上位10％が総利用額の45％を占める」と加えると、顧客行動をより現実的に説明できます。

「平均顧客」と聞いたら、その顧客が本当に存在するかを考えるべきです。数学的に正しい平均でも、実際の顧客をほとんど表していないことがあります。

施策では顧客ごとに必要なactionが違います。低頻度層とheavy userには別のofferが必要かもしれません。meanだけでstoryを作る前にdataの形を見ることが重要です。

vocabulary.usage: The average may not describe a real customer.
Compare the mean with the median.
Check the shape of the distribution.
Use percentiles to describe customer spread.
Avoid designing for an imaginary average customer.

business.term: The average is useful, but it does not necessarily describe a typical customer.
business.explanation: 用來提醒團隊不要把平均值當成真實典型人物。
